extracted.intended_audience: public relations students and practitioners (PR professionals and managers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for planning, writing, budgeting, pretesting, implementing, and evaluating public relations programs; includes how to define publics, write measurable objectives, select strategies/tactics, coordinate action and communication, and secure management buy-in.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information forefending
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent to which a communicator fends off certain information in advance by judging its value and relevance for a given problem-solving task.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a college student who is pro-choice will disregard a pro-life brochure because she deems it irrational or irrelevant to her perspective. Use this concept to anticipate what information target publics will ignore.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information permitting
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent to which a communicator accepts any information related to a problem-solving task.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a high-school student planning to go to college will review any and all information pertaining to the college-application process. Use this behavior to identify publics likely to seek and accept information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information forwarding
rubrics_metrics.description: The voluntary, premeditated, and self-propelled giving of information to others about problems and solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and leverage publics likely to forward messages (e.g., influencers who proactively share content).

rubrics_metrics.name: Information sharing
rubrics_metrics.description: The involuntary, reactive, and unplanned giving of information to others, usually only when solicited by others to give an opinion or to share an experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize contexts where audiences will only share when asked; design opportunities to solicit their input or testimonials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design programs to facilitate problem-solvers' communicative actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations efforts are more effective when practitioners understand and facilitate problem-solvers’ communicative actions by identifying publics that seek out, give, and select information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan activities that match publics' tendencies to acquire, select, and transmit information (timing, channels, content relevance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographics as a public-definition approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Use natural or political boundaries (ZIP codes, area codes, city limits, county lines, voting districts) to indicate where to find people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful for selecting media outlets and allocating program resources by population density, but gives little insight into differences within boundaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demographics as a public-definition approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Segment publics by gender, income, age, marital status, education, and similar individual characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most frequently used attributes; helpful for an initial cut but insufficient without situation-specific information about involvement or effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychographics (VALS) as a public-definition approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Segment based on psychological and lifestyle characteristics (values, personality, 'psychological maturity').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful when combined with attributes that tie segments to the particular situation; alone it often lacks situational relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Covert power as a public-definition approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify behind-the-scenes political or economic power-holders who exert influence across situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires observation, interviews, and document analysis to find these actors who are not overtly visible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Position as a public-definition approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify publics by positions held (roles) rather than individual attributes; roles make people important players in a situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use role-based identification to find those whose positions confer influence relevant to program goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reputation as a public-definition approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify 'knowledgeables' or 'influentials' based on others’ perceptions—opinion leaders defined by the situation’s participants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish this from covert power or externally-imposed opinion-leader definitions; reputation is situationally assigned by other stakeholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Membership as a public-definition approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Use organizational rosters, affiliations, or group membership to identify publics involved in a situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Members often receive controlled media from the organization or network-based communications tied to their affiliation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role in the decision process as a public-definition approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Observe the decision-making process to learn who influences and makes decisions in the situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Helps identify the most active publics—those who actually take action and communicate—where behavior matters more than personal attributes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication behavior as a public-definition approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Document with whom participants share information, from whom they seek information, and what media they use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These observations guide identification of thought/opinion leaders and selection of media to reach target publics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish goals from objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Goals are broad, summative statements of overall program outcomes and timelines; objectives represent specific knowledge, opinion, and behavioral outcomes to be achieved for each target public (key results).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use goals to state the desired overall result; use objectives as measurable, time-bound steps that, when achieved across publics, accomplish the goal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Management by Objectives (MBO) for PR
rubrics_metrics.description: MBO systematically specifies outcomes (consequences, results, impact) as criteria for selecting strategies, monitoring performance, and evaluating program effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Articulate clear PR goals and objectives so PR activities fit into organizational management processes and decision making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program objectives must include Target Public
rubrics_metrics.description: Objectives must specify the public being targeted, as defined earlier in planning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the target public is omitted, implementation becomes difficult because practitioners won’t know who to reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program objectives must specify Outcome (learn–feel–do)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each objective should spell out a single specific outcome in one of three categories: knowledge (aware/know/understand), predispositional (how people feel), or behavioral (what people do).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the causal sequence Information Gain ⇒ Opinion Change ⇒ Behavioral Change; behavioral change typically requires prior opinion support and informational support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program objectives must include Measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Objectives must state the magnitude of change or level to be maintained in measurable, quantifiable terms that are realistic and consistent with resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use experience, judgment, and situation-analysis research to set outcome levels; without benchmark data, rely on informed judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program objectives must include Target Date
rubrics_metrics.description: Objectives should specify the target date by which the outcome is to be achieved and follow logical sequencing when one outcome depends on another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dates guide scheduling of communications and events and determine when implementation is finished and evaluation can begin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid activity- or tactic-focused 'objectives' (common pitfall)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many so-called objectives describe the tactic (means) rather than the consequence (ends)—e.g., 'To mail out 12 monthly issues' or 'To inform people about…'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask, 'Is this something the organization needs to do?' If yes, the statement likely describes a tactic, not an objective. A proper objective should describe an impact in a target public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategy vs. Tactics distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Strategy: the overall concept, approach, or general plan designed to achieve an objective. Tactics: the actual events, media, and methods used to implement the strategy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select strategy to achieve a particular outcome (goal/objective); choose tactics as the steps on the ladder to execute the strategy (John Beardsley: 'Strategy is a ladder leading to a goal. Tactics are the steps on the ladder.').

rubrics_metrics.name: Action strategies should include internal corrective actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Action strategies typically include changes in policies, procedures, products, services, and behavior—internal changes designed to achieve objectives and respond to publics’ needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corrective actions should be taken before external communications; example: fix recruiting processes internally before external recruitment messaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action as an open-systems, socially responsible response
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations action is 'socially responsible acts taken by public relations departments or other parts of the organization with your counsel.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actions should serve mutual interests of the organization and its publics and be based on understanding how organizational outputs contribute to PR problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action before communication (coordinate, don't contradict)
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizations must implement corrective internal actions before reaching out externally, coordinating action and communication so they do not contradict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You cannot apologize for wrongdoing while continuing it; first stop the behavior, plan and explain cleanup, then communicate how future risks will be prevented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public Relations Strategic Planning Outline (plan components)
rubrics_metrics.description: A final public relations plan typically includes: The Problem; Situation Analysis (internal and external); The Problem Statement; Program Goal Statement; Target Publics; Objectives; Action Strategy and Tactics; Communication Strategy and Tactics; Coordinating Action and Communication; Program Implementation Plans; Evaluation Plans; Feedback and Program Adjustment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this structured outline (Exhibit 12.4) as a checklist when writing proposals/plans to ensure the plan is coherent, acceptable to management, and realistic to implement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budgeting control factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Budgets generally relate to one of four control factors: (1) total income/funds available, (2) 'competitive necessity' (matching/exceeding competitors), (3) overall task or goal set for the organization, and (4) profit or surplus over expenses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each basis has implications: percentage-of-revenue methods, risky competitor-matching, task/goal-aligned budgeting, or fluctuating profit-based allocations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budgeting: itemize fixed and variable costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Specialists should estimate and itemize variable costs (printing, speakers, travel, etc.) and add them to fixed costs (salaries, benefits, overhead) to develop the budget.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher-level managers evaluate and adjust unit budgets to fit total available funds; budgeting is usually a multi-level negotiation process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budgeting guidelines: know costs; tie to results; use software
rubrics_metrics.description: Three practical budgeting rules: (1) Know the exact cost of what you propose to buy; (2) Communicate the budget in terms of what it costs to achieve specific results; (3) Use software to manage programs and cash flow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Managers want to know how much to achieve goals/objectives (not line-item minutiae). Use spreadsheets and project-level tracking to estimate cash flow and monitor expenditures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use budgets as management tools and link to performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Budgets should be used to schedule staff resources, contract services, track project costs, and establish accountability; they shape relationships with clients and top management.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to budgets when assessing performance; review budgets frequently with clients and management and link costs to staff performance and program outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pretesting program elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Once the strategic plan is formulated, it should be tried on a pilot basis using qualitative and quantitative tools (interviews with opinion leaders, focus groups, controlled lab tests, field tests).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pretests estimate how elements will work, compare alternatives, and detect backlash effects. Use response analysis (sample audience reaction) to catch problematic content (examples of OSHA booklet failures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Message and material pretesting to ensure understandability
rubrics_metrics.description: Pretesting helps increase the understandability of information for intended audiences; symbolism that is clear to creators may be unintelligible or inappropriate for recipients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pretest even small details (e.g., images that might offend cultural norms) to avoid large-scale embarrassment or cultural errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cautions about pretesting (time-lag and representativeness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public opinion is dynamic; an idea that worked in a pretest might fail on wide release due to seasonality, changing concerns, or overpowering events that alter opinion climate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure pretest conditions and subjects are representative of the program's target publics and current conditions before relying on pretest results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Getting buy-in by demonstrating impact on organizational goals/bottom line
rubrics_metrics.description: To gain management/client approval, demonstrate how the program will help achieve organizational goals, affect the bottom line, and protect reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Managers expect PR to manage environmental threats, enhance competitive edge, and protect reputation; tie PR objectives to sales, profits, market share, talent attraction, donor appeal, or stock price as relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation and persuasion tips for selling the plan
rubrics_metrics.description: When presenting the plan: explain problems in terms of harm if unattended; explain immediate remedial measures in relation to long-term plans; use case examples, precedents, and survey results; eliminate personal opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep explanations short and to the point, be decisive and have conviction, and focus on future compatibility with leaders' concerns (Lukaszewski: 'the trusted strategic advisor can only be a force for tomorrow').

rubrics_metrics.name: Familiarize colleagues and collaborators after approval
rubrics_metrics.description: After a program is approved, practitioners must familiarize colleagues and collaborators with what will follow so they can do their part and solicit support from subordinates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid leaving important collaborators uninformed (e.g., outside counselors excluded from planning); ensure everyone responsible has the objectives and plan so implementation is coordinated.
